text:
How does a database find one row among ten million almost instantly? Usually it uses an index. It works like the index at the back of a textbook: you look up the topic and go straight to the right page instead of flipping through every one.

Most database indexes are built on a B-tree, a structure that makes lookups O(log n). In practice, doubling your data adds about one more step to a search instead of doubling the work. In one real case, a query on a 10M-row table went from 2.1 seconds to 4 milliseconds after it got an index, and users notice a difference that big.

The cost shows up on writes. Every insert and update also has to update the index, which can slow writes by about 15%. The rest of this post covers how indexes work, when they help, and how to decide which ones are worth that cost.
